title: ‘Sickening’: Over-65s warn they’ll dump private health
full_text:
The number of older Australians who would cancel their private health insurance because of the Albanese government’s reforms is eight times what Labor initially anticipated, according to new research.
As the government struggles to push through its contentious rebate cut for over-65s in the final sitting fortnight of the year, an Ipsos survey of 2148 private health policy holders – about a quarter of whom were aged 65 and older – found 12.1 per cent of that age group would drop their cover tomorrow if the overhaul were to proceed.
That finding is much higher than the 1.6 per cent – or roughly 44,000 people – in the 2028-29 financial year estimated by the Albanese government to cancel their insurance.
Departmental analysis shows the 44,000 figure is expected to blow out to 78,000 just a year later. Another 12.2 per cent of over-65s would downgrade their cover, 8.9 per cent would increase their excess or reduce benefits, and 11.3 per cent would switch insurers to find lower-cost options, while 33 per cent of older Australians wouldn’t make any changes.
In total, almost half of over-65s surveyed indicated they’d make changes to their private health insurance arrangements.
The poll was commissioned by Members Health Fund Alliance, the national peak body for not-for-profit and member-owned health funds, ahead of any final attempts by Labor to legislate its reforms, which would save the government $3bn to be redirected into aged care beds and services.
The Greens are standing firm against the changes unless the government is willing to carve out all pensioners, which would force Labor to forgo half of its savings.
The polling also found more than 80 per cent of Australians aged 65+ either strongly opposed or somewhat opposed the policy, while just 17 per cent of 18 to 24-year-olds were against it as well as 26 per cent of 25 to 34-year-olds.
Opposition increased among older Australians and support was strongest in younger people (44 per cent for the 18 to 24 cohort).
“When more than 80 per cent of Australians aged 65 plus oppose it, parliament is entitled to ask whether this policy is another one this government has got seriously wrong,” Members Health chief executive Matthew Koce said.
“This will hurt our most vulnerable in the community most likely to need healthcare. We are talking about grandparents who may be forced to give up cover because they can no longer afford it, leaving them more reliant on an already overwhelmed public health system.
“These are Australians who have done exactly what successive governments have encouraged them to do. They have maintained private health insurance, paid their premiums and helped take pressure off public hospitals. Now, they are being asked to accept less support at precisely the stage of life when they are more likely to need healthcare.” Seventy-nine-year-old Michael McShane, a full-rate pensioner who lives in Newcastle, took out private health insurance in 1965 when he began working and has always held the maximum cover.
With serious health conditions, including prostate cancer, Mr McShane said his medical costs had increased by $100,000 in the last few years and he was reliant on the more generous private health insurance rebate for over-65s.
Under the government’s changes, Mr McShane could be expected to have his gold cover premium increase by up to 21.3 per cent from April 1, based on industry estimates.
“I’ve got to rethink the whole cost-of-living situation because you’ve got to budget pretty tightly and any change in that income has a dramatic effect because I’m on a fixed income. There’s no way I can earn extra money to pay for extra costs,” he said.
“If the costs are that way, I’ve got to go under the public system. The cost of that is going to be enormous. You’re not going to get the service. The hospitals will be overloaded.” A long-time Liberal voter, Mr McShane said he wouldn’t be able to maintain top cover if there was any decrease to the government rebate he received, adding that he felt as though older Australians were “under attack”.
“Health is the most important thing in your life because if you haven’t got good health, you’ve got nothing,” Mr McShane said.
“As you get older, one thing I have realised is that you really start to get the benefit of the private health insurance because you start to get into quite serious medical conditions, which are very costly and which, if you didn’t have the fund, I certainly wouldn’t be able to undertake that medical treatment. It would have a devastating effect on me.” Health and Ageing Minister Mark Butler has repeatedly said reversing the more generous Howard-era rebates for over 65s was not something he wanted to do but was necessary to fund aged care. “I just don’t think I was in a position to maintain a subsidy that was paid at different rates depending on age rather than income when we have to lean so heavily into finding new aged care services,” he said on ABC Adelaide earlier this year.
